bodies.the-agentic-enterprise:
For most of the past few years, enterprise AI has meant software that suggests: a draft email, a summarised document, a recommended next step. A human read the output and decided what to do. AI agents change that relationship. An agent is given a goal, a set of tools and some boundaries, and it decides which actions to take — querying a database, filing a ticket, updating a record — often across several steps.

That shift from suggestion to action is small in a demo and enormous in production. It changes how software must be permissioned, tested, observed and governed. This article sets out what organisations deploying agents are learning, and the questions leaders should be asking before scaling them.

What we mean by an “agent”

The term is used loosely, so it helps to be precise. In this article, an agent is a system in which a language model chooses actions from a defined set of tools, observes the results, and continues until it reaches a goal or a stopping condition. Three properties distinguish it from a chatbot:

  • Tool use. The model can call functions — search, read, write, or trigger workflows — rather than only producing text.
  • Multi-step planning. The model decides the sequence of actions itself, adapting to intermediate results.
  • Delegated authority. Some actions take effect without a human approving each one.

It is the third property that makes agents an organisational question rather than only a technical one.

A spectrum of autonomy

Few production systems are fully autonomous. Most sit somewhere on a spectrum, and choosing the right point for each workflow is the most important design decision teams make.

LevelWhat the agent doesTypical use
AssistProposes actions; a human executes themDrafting replies, preparing reports
ApproveExecutes after explicit human approvalRefunds, account changes, outbound messages
SuperviseExecutes within limits; humans review samplesTicket triage, data enrichment
AutonomousExecutes and reports outcomesLow-risk, easily reversible internal tasks

Permissions become product design

Traditional software permissions are attached to people. Agents need permissions of their own, and those permissions must be narrower than the user they act for. An agent that summarises a customer’s account does not need permission to close it.

Teams that do this well define tools around business actions rather than raw system access. Instead of granting an agent general database write access, they expose a single issue_credit(account_id, amount, reason) function with its own limits, logging and approval rules.

// Illustrative tool definition with built-in guardrails
{
  "name": "issue_credit",
  "description": "Issue a service credit to a customer account.",
  "limits": { "max_amount": 50, "currency": "USD" },
  "requires_approval_above": 20,
  "audit": true
}

This pattern keeps the blast radius of a mistake small and makes the agent’s capabilities legible to the people responsible for it.

The question is not whether the model is smart enough. It is whether the system around the model is designed for the moments when it is wrong.— A recurring theme in conversations with teams running agents in production

Evaluation moves from outputs to trajectories

Evaluating a chatbot means judging its answers. Evaluating an agent means judging its path: which tools it chose, in what order, with which arguments, and whether it stopped at the right moment. A correct final answer reached through an unsafe action is still a failure.

Building useful evaluation sets

  1. Collect real tasks from the workflow, including the awkward edge cases experienced staff remember.
  2. Define what a good trajectory looks like for each task, not only the expected result.
  3. Include tasks where the correct behaviour is to stop and escalate.
  4. Re-run the full set whenever prompts, tools or models change.

Our guide to evaluating LLM applications covers the mechanics in more depth.

Observability is non-negotiable

When an agent does something unexpected, teams need to reconstruct exactly what happened: the instructions it received, the context it retrieved, each tool call and each result. Without this trace, debugging becomes guesswork and accountability becomes impossible.

Practical baseline: log every tool call with its arguments, result, latency and the identity on whose behalf the agent acted. Retain traces long enough to investigate complaints, and treat them as sensitive data.

Measuring value honestly

It is tempting to report the number of tasks an agent completes. A more honest measure compares the full cost of a workflow — including human review, error correction and escalations — before and after the agent is introduced. Some of the most successful deployments automate less than expected but remove the most tedious steps entirely.

Questions leaders should ask

  • Which actions can this agent take, and which are reversible?
  • Who is accountable when it makes a mistake, and how will we know?
  • What does the evaluation set contain, and when was it last updated?
  • How does cost per completed task compare with the previous process?

What comes next

Agents are not a replacement for well-designed software; they are a new kind of component inside it. The organisations getting real value are the ones treating agent design as a discipline that combines product thinking, security engineering and operational rigour. That combination — more than any single model release — will decide which deployments last.
bodies.platform-engineering-paved-roads:
Every engineering organisation eventually reaches the point where each team is solving the same infrastructure problems slightly differently. Platform engineering promises a fix: a shared internal platform that makes the right way the easy way. Yet many platforms end up as expensive portals that developers route around.

The difference between those outcomes is rarely technology. It is whether the platform team behaves like a product team.

Paved roads, not gates

A paved road is an opinionated, well-supported path for a common task — creating a service, deploying it, adding observability. Teams may leave the road, but they take on the maintenance burden when they do. A gate, by contrast, forces every team through a process regardless of fit.

  • Paved roads earn adoption by being faster than the alternative.
  • Gates earn compliance, and often resentment.

Treat developers as users

Successful platform teams interview developers, watch them use the tooling and measure friction directly. They maintain a roadmap, publish release notes and retire features that nobody uses.

Metrics that matter

MetricWhat it tells you
Time to first deployHow quickly a new service reaches production
Voluntary adoptionWhether teams choose the platform when they could opt out
Developer satisfactionPerceived friction, measured with short regular surveys

Start with one golden path

The most reliable way to start is to pick a single high-frequency workflow — often “create and deploy a new service” — and make it excellent. A scaffolding command can encode many decisions at once:

platform new service --name billing-events --template event-consumer
# creates repo, CI pipeline, dashboards, alerts and on-call rota
If developers need a meeting to use your platform, it is not a platform yet.

Avoid common traps

  1. Building a portal before the underlying automation works.
  2. Abstracting so heavily that debugging requires the platform team.
  3. Measuring success by features shipped rather than friction removed.

Cost visibility is increasingly part of the platform’s job too; see our playbook on FinOps for engineers.

The long game

Platforms compound. Each paved road makes the next one cheaper to build and easier to adopt. The teams that succeed are patient, user-obsessed and willing to delete what isn’t working.
bodies.lights-out-factory-myth:
The image is compelling: a factory running in darkness, robots working through the night without a single person on site. It appears in investor presentations and conference keynotes. On real shop floors, it remains rare — and chasing it can distract from the improvements that matter most.

Why full autonomy is rare

Highly automated lines exist, particularly for stable, high-volume products. But most manufacturers operate in a world of product variation, supply disruption and equipment that ages unevenly. Each of those introduces exceptions, and exceptions still need people.

  • Product mix changes faster than automation can be reconfigured.
  • Maintenance and quality issues require judgement on the spot.
  • Material variation creates edge cases rigid systems handle poorly.

What is actually working

The plants showing measurable gains tend to combine modest automation with excellent information flow.

Connected equipment and visible data

Connecting machines so that downtime, scrap and throughput are visible in near real time often delivers more value than adding new robots. Operators and supervisors can respond to problems in minutes rather than shifts.

Targeted automation

Automation applied to the most repetitive, dangerous or ergonomically difficult tasks frees skilled people for problem-solving. Collaborative robots are well suited here — see our report on cobots and assembly work.

ApproachTypical payback driverMain risk
Machine connectivityReduced unplanned downtimeData not acted upon
Targeted cobotsLabour reallocation, ergonomicsPoor task selection
Full line automationThroughput on stable productsInflexibility when demand shifts
The plants that impressed me most were not the darkest. They were the ones where everyone could see what was happening.

People remain central

As automation increases, roles shift towards monitoring, maintenance and continuous improvement. That transition requires training and deliberate job design; it does not happen by default.

A practical roadmap

  1. Instrument the constraint: find and measure the bottleneck operation.
  2. Make losses visible to the people who can act on them.
  3. Automate the tasks people least want to do.
  4. Build data foundations that later initiatives — like digital twins — can rely on.

The lights-out factory may arrive for some products. For most manufacturers, the better goal is a factory where problems surface early and people have the time and tools to solve them.
